claims.claim: Christianity originated in the early first century CE, rooted in the life, teachings, and death of Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish teacher in Roman Judaea; the movement that formed around him grew into the world's largest religion.
Christianity is the world's largest religion, with over two billion adherents, and one of the most geographically widespread faiths.

Core beliefs as the tradition describes them: Christians identify Jesus as the Christ, the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, and as the Son of God; the Trinity (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) is the mainstream creedal formulation of one God in three persons; incarnation, crucifixion, and resurrection are central claims; salvation and grace are central themes.

The Christian Bible is a collection in two major parts: the Old Testament, corresponding largely to the Hebrew Bible and essential to Christianity, and the New Testament, which includes the Gospels, the accounts of Jesus' life and teaching.

Central Christian practices include worship in churches (with spiritual leaders called priests or ministers), prayer, and the rites of baptism (initiation with water) and the Eucharist (Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper, recalling Jesus' last meal with his followers); the liturgical year includes Christmas and Easter, which follows Lent and commemorates the resurrection.

Christianity is internally diverse: the major branches are Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox (with Oriental Orthodoxy), and Protestant; the schism of 1054 divided the Western church from the Eastern churches, and the 16th-century Reformation produced the Protestant churches; movements such as Pentecostalism, Charismatic Christianity, and Evangelicalism are significant, and there are numerous independent churches worldwide.

Christianity's demographic center has shifted south: more than 1.3 billion Christians (about 61%) live in the Global South versus about 860 million (39%) in the Global North; sub-Saharan Africa's Christian share of its regional population rose from 9% in 1910 to 63% in 2010; Europe's share of the world's Christians fell from about two-thirds in 1910 to about a quarter by 2010.

Christianity has generated a culture: in Britannica's framing it is a tradition of faith and the culture that faith has created, with the church as the community of believers; its influence on art, ethics, and institutions is described generally.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Precise dates for the life of Jesus
positions: Britannica: Jesus of Nazareth lived in the 1st century CE; born in Bethlehem and raised in Nazareth; public ministry as an itinerant preacher and healer beginning in his early 30s
Scholarly estimates of exact birth and death years vary (commonly cited ranges differ by several years either side of the conventional dates)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the hedged historical framing — early first century CE, a Jewish teacher in Roman Judaea — and assigns no exact birth or death year.

positions: Catholic and Orthodox traditions typically number seven sacraments, with baptism and the Eucharist at the center
Many Protestant traditions emphasize baptism and the Eucharist specifically, sometimes calling them ordinances
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names baptism and the Eucharist as the rites most widely shared across traditions and notes that churches number and name them differently.

positions: Historically centered in Europe: about two-thirds of Christians lived in Europe in 1910
Pew Research (2011): more than 1.3 billion Christians (61%) now live in the Global South
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the documented demographic shift rather than a fixed characterization: Christianity began in the Middle East and now has its majority of adherents in the Global South.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft (public/content/phase-3/lessons.json) contained only generic boilerplate ('Christianity is a foundational concept in Religious Studies') and no factual claims; none of it was carried into the lesson.
correctionsNeeded: Discarded the machine-generated boilerplate draft entirely and replaced it with source-verified content.
Hedged the dating of Jesus' life to 'early first century CE' rather than assigning exact years, per conflicting evidence.
Presented Christian beliefs (Trinity, incarnation, crucifixion, resurrection, salvation) strictly as claims of the tradition, never adjudicated.
Named the internal diversity of Christianity (Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, Pentecostalism and other movements) explicitly instead of treating Christianity as one uniform church.
Used Pew Research's documented figures for the Global South shift rather than a general 'Christianity is growing in Africa' claim.
Described the Bible's structure and the Gospels in general terms and never quoted scripture.

sourceRecords.title: Christianity
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A per the assignment brief. Read via an Internet Archive capture (web.archive.org/web/2026/https://www.britannica.com/topic/Christianity) on 2026-08-21 because the live site returns HTTP 403 to automated fetch; article marked last updated Aug. 14, 2026. Supports: Christianity as a major religion rooted in the life, teachings, and death of Jesus of Nazareth in the 1st century CE; the world's largest and most geographically widespread faith with over two billion followers; Jesus Christ described as the incarnate Son of God whose life, death, and resurrection offer salvation, with public ministry as an itinerant preacher and healer beginning in his early 30s; early followers seeing Jesus as the Messiah and Son of God; the Holy Trinity as doctrine and the Trinitarian invocation in baptism; baptism as a sacrament of admission using water, and the Eucharist (Holy Communion, the Lord's Supper) as a central act of worship derived from the Last Supper; Easter following Lent and commemorating the resurrection; Christmas traditions; the major branches of Roman Catholicism, Eastern Orthodoxy, Oriental Orthodoxy, and Protestantism; the Schism of 1054 and the Reformation; Pentecostalism, Charismatic Christianity, Evangelicalism, and fundamentalism as significant movements with numerous independent churches worldwide; Christianity as 'a tradition of faith and the culture that faith has created'; the church as the community of believers; the Hebrew Bible as essential to Christianity; the Gospels depicting Jesus as teacher and savior. Facts synthesized in original wording; no Britannica prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: 15.2 World Religions — Introduction to Sociology 3e
sourceRecords.notes: Existing source-registry record reused with identical id and URL. Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: Christianity as today the largest religion in the world; it began 2,000 years ago in the Middle East with Jesus of Nazareth, a leader who taught his followers caritas (charity) or treating others as you would like to be treated yourself; the Bible as the sacred text for Christians; the Christian notion of the Holy Trinity (God, Jesus, Holy Spirit) and scholarly discussion of how it relates to strict definitions of monotheism; the shared sacred stories of Jews, Christians, and Muslims, with Christians believing the son of God / messiah already appeared in Jesus Christ while Jewish and Muslim traditions see the prophecy as not yet fulfilled; the Roman Catholic Church's historical borrowing of organizational principles. Facts synthesized; no OpenStax wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Global Christianity – A Report on the Size and Distribution of the World's Christian Population (Executive Summary)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). A comprehensive demographic study of more than 200 countries. Supports: 2.18 billion Christians of all ages worldwide in 2010, nearly a third of the estimated global population of 6.9 billion; Christians as by far the world's largest religious group; more than 1.3 billion Christians (61%) in the Global South versus about 860 million (39%) in the Global North; a century ago the Global North contained more than four times as many Christians as the Global South; in 1910 about two-thirds of the world's Christians lived in Europe versus about a quarter (26%) in 2010; sub-Saharan Africa's Christian share of its regional population climbing from 9% in 1910 to 63% in 2010; about one in four Christians living in sub-Saharan Africa (24%); the top-ten countries by Christian population spanning the Americas, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and sub-Saharan Africa. Statistics reported in own words; no Pew wording reproduced.
